label: MiniMax M3.1 Flash
output:
Here's the letter. I kept everything from your notes and built it around her — the kitchen as the place where the real talks happened, the silliness, and the Dec 5 ending you wanted. I put two laugh beats in on purpose (the $20 and the pager one), plus the crib league for good measure.

---

**Dear Nana,**

I'm writing this Thursday night so Denise can read it to you Friday, while the two of you sit in the kitchen with the radio going, because that's where we did all the real talking in this family and I wasn't about to change the format at the last minute.

Fair warning: it's long. If Denise gets teary about halfway through, hand her the letter and finish it yourself. That's what I'd do.

First, the thing I've been carrying around all week, which is that I'm not going to be there Saturday. I'm on call that week — primary, the whole week, and I couldn't find anybody to trade with me. I know people keep telling me it's fine, and maybe it is, mostly, but I'm going to say it out loud anyway because you raised half the family in that kitchen and I think you're allowed one honest paragraph.

Here's the joke, though, and I didn't see it until I started writing this. You ask me every single time we talk if anything broke. Last Christmas my pager went off in the middle of dinner and you looked at the table and said, "Is the internet broken again?" and then you wanted to know if I fixed it. And now that's literally my job. I am the person they call when it breaks and then they call me again when I haven't fixed it fast enough. So I spent fifteen years becoming the guy who fixes broken things, and this week the thing that's breaking is me not being in your hallway, and I couldn't fix that one. That's a strange sentence. I'm going to stop there.

Denise is going to be there, though, and Denise is an angel, and I'm going to be nicer to her than I have been all year.

Now. Elmwood Terrace.

I looked at the pictures you sent and it looks genuinely nice, Nana. Second floor, so you're not on the ground with everybody else's laundry and the pigeons. And the view is a parking lot and a big maple, which — I'm sorry, but you've gone from a driveway and a hedge to a maple tree, that's an upgrade. I'll take it. You did well.

And I want to say this plainly, because I don't think anybody's said it to you in a way that stuck: I'm proud of you. Not proud in a sweet way, not the way people say it at a retirement party with a certificate in their hand. Proud in the way where you picked this place, you signed the papers, you packed your own life into a plan, and nobody made you do it. You did it yourself. Six years you've been keeping a whole house going on your own since Grandpa died, and at eighty-eight you looked around and said *this is done*, and you went and found somewhere better, and you did it without anybody twisting your arm. That's not a thing that just happens. That's a woman who ran a house for fifty-one years and then decided, on purpose, what she wanted next. I'm proud of you for that. I wanted to write it down so it's in ink and Denise can't accidentally lose it.

The house on Kathleen Street. Fifty-one years. You moved in as a young woman with a husband and a baby and you lived there through every single era of my life — the summer I was seven and you taught me cribbage in that kitchen and refused, every single time, to let me win. You know what I remember most about that? Not the cards. That you taught me at seven and you let me sit there for hours with a bad hand and a good teacher and you never once threw a card down and said, "here, take this one, you're doing great." Not once. You just played like I was a real person and expected me to keep up, and I did, mostly, and when I didn't I'd hear about it for a week. That's how you taught me everything, by the way. That's the whole method. You never coddled anybody in that kitchen.

And then I skunked you. I was fifteen. I was fifteen years old and I finally caught you and you handed over your cards without a word and got up and made me a whole pan of butter tarts. A whole pan. Not one tart, a *pan*, because you were that kind of winner. I still think about that pan more than I think about most things. I think about it a lot, actually.

And I think about the little television in the kitchen, the one with the rabbit ears, and how I was supposed to dry the dishes if I wanted to stay up and watch the Expos or the Jays. You were strict about the dishes. Not a dish left in the sink, no half-dried anything, no "I'll do it tomorrow." Do it now or you don't get the game. And I'd do them, and I'd dry them, and I'd put them away, and then I'd sit on the floor with my back against the cabinet and fall asleep forty minutes into the ninth inning and wake up to the radio and the dishes put away and you and Grandpa not saying a word about it, because you weren't going to wake me up after I earned it. Every summer. Fifty-one years of summers. I don't think you ever once thought of it as anything special. It was just the house. It was just the deal.

And then the back steps. Six in the morning, tea, sitting out there in whatever the weather was. You never talked until the cup was done. I know that sounds like nothing. It isn't nothing. That was you letting the morning happen first, before the day got going, before you were anybody's grandmother or anybody's Nana, just a woman with a cup of tea on the steps. And I'd come out and sit down and you'd pour me one without asking, and neither of us would say anything for a while, and I never once thought to wonder why you were like that. Now I think about it all the time. I think about how you had a whole life in that house that wasn't about anybody else, and I got to sit in it, and I didn't know that was a gift.

The $20 bill. I need to tell you this story because it makes me laugh every time. I got the job in Toronto, and in the mail — actual mail, Nana, this is how old we are — there was a card with a twenty-dollar bill taped to it and a note in your handwriting that said "for pizza, you look thin on the computer." Taped. With tape. I still have that card in a drawer in my apartment. I keep it. That's not even a joke, I actually keep it. I paid for a lot of pizza with it, over a lot of years, and you were right, I did look thin on the computer, and I never once ate a slice of pizza in that city without thinking about you and your kitchen and the fact that you'd decided I needed feeding from three hundred kilometres away.

You raised half the family in that kitchen. I want that said. Not the version where people say it and everybody nods and moves on — I want it actually said, in writing, by somebody who was one of the kids in that room. That room was where people got made. That's where people learned to sit at a table and lose at cribbage and eat too much and get told to dry the dishes if they wanted to stay up late. That was the machine. Everything good about our family came out of that room, and I know it, and you know it, and I'm writing it down so it's on the record.

But it's not a funeral. I want to be clear about that, because I know what this week feels like from your side too. This isn't the house ending. The house is a house. It's going to be there, and I'm going to drive past it in December, and somebody else's kid is going to be in that kitchen with a rabbit-eared television and no idea how lucky they are.

Elmwood's got a cribbage league, Nana. I know this because you told me and you said it like it was a selling feature, which, honestly? Fair. It is. You could have gone anywhere. You could have picked a place with a putting green. You picked the place with the league. That is the correct decision and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. You're eighty-eight years old, you're still beating the church ladies on Tuesdays, and now you're going to walk into a new building and beat a bunch of strangers, and I am going to hear about it, and I will never once let you forget it.

Denise is taking the cuckoo clock and the cedar chest. I'm sorry about the cuckoo clock — that thing was Dad's and yours and it was loud and it was always slightly wrong and I have no idea how it's going to survive the move, but I'm glad it's going with you. It should go with you. It should be in the new place, ticking away at whatever the wrong time it thinks it is.

And I asked Denise for the cribbage board. Just so you know. The board, Nana. I'm taking that with me on December 5th, and I'm bringing it up to Elmwood Terrace, and if you've got a league game scheduled that weekend I would very much like to be in it. Rotation's done by then, I promise. I'll be there Friday evening, we'll have it in my car the whole drive up, and December 5th I'm sitting at a table at your new place with your board and my hands and I'm going to skunk you one more time, because I've been practising on my own hands for fifteen years and you have no idea what's coming.

Read this in the kitchen tomorrow night. Say it out loud if you want, or let Denise read it, or just hold it. And then on Saturday, when you walk into Elmwood Terrace for the last time with your own keys, remember: you picked this. You did it yourself. Nobody made you.

Your grandson, who will see you on December 5th with a cribbage board under his arm.

---

Two small notes: I left the "your house is done" thought in there about Walt, and the "six years keeping the house going" line is the one that carries the pride without making it a funeral. If you want it warmer or less sharp at the opening, the middle paragraph about the pager is the easiest to trim — but honestly it's the bit that earns the on-call apology instead of just excusing it. And read it to yourself out loud once before you send it to Denise; that's how you'd catch the choke.
